## Chapter Summary

Descriptive analytics summarizes what happened, and diagnostic analytics explains why. Much of what accountants produce, from comparative statements to variance reports, is descriptive, and diagnostic work begins when a summary shows a change that nobody expected. This chapter moved from one to the other with four families of Excel tools: statistical functions, conditional aggregation, PivotTables, and a margin bridge.

Statistical functions describe a column with a single number. AVERAGE and MEDIAN measure its center, and a mean well above the median signals a right-skewed distribution, the usual shape of accounting populations. STDEV.S and STDEV.P measure its spread, and MIN, MAX, and PERCENTILE.INC describe its extremes and serve as data checks. MEDIAN, STDEV.S, and PERCENTILE.INC accept no criteria, so FILTER supplies them with part of a table. Because a statistic can hide the shape of the data it summarizes, it should be read alongside the data and calculated separately for groups that behave differently. Conditional aggregation functions, SUMIFS, COUNTIFS, AVERAGEIFS, MINIFS, and MAXIFS, calculate results for the rows that meet criteria kept in cells. They fail silently, returning zero for a misspelled or missing category, so every summary by category should be compared with a control total.

PivotTables build a summary from fields placed in their Rows, Columns, Values, and Filters areas, with totals for every row and column. Value field settings choose the calculation and format, Show Values As displays the same values as shares or changes, and calculated fields define measures such as margins. A calculated field works on the sums of its fields, so it suits ratios of totals but not products of fields, which belong in the source as custom or calculated columns. PivotTables summarize a cache that must be refreshed after the source changes, formulas should refer to them with GETPIVOTDATA, and a summary of the ledger by period must exclude the year-end closing entries.

Diagnosis drills down, compares, and decomposes. A margin bridge breaks the change in margin between two periods into volume, mix, price, and cost effects that add up exactly to the change, and the level at which it is calculated affects how the change divides among them. Applied to Charles River, the bridge showed that the Furniture margin at standard cost fell from the third quarter of fiscal 2026 to the fourth because promotional discounts, mostly from the Furniture Seasonal Promotion, more than doubled, while volume, mix, list prices, and standard costs changed little. A finding like this should state its evidence, start from an expectation, and claim no more than the evidence supports.
